newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn expects to meet EEC telecoms licence deadline.
newsitem.headline: Bonn expects to meet EEC telecoms licence deadline.

text.p: Germany has not awarded licences for alternative telecommunications networks as required by the European Commission in June, but it still expects to meet the November deadline, the Bonn post ministry said on Friday.

Responding to a complaint filed by six telecoms companies in Brussels, the post ministry said it had so far received some 30 applications for alternative communications networks and that a legal formality was holding up awarding some licences.

"We still need to pass a legal ordinance that regulates the charges for such licences," said Christian Hoppe, spokesman at the postal ministry. "We are confident that this issue will be cleared up and it is still possible to meet the deadline."
It was not clear how many of the licences would eventually be awarded, but Hoppe said there would probably be at least two awarded by the November 1 deadline set by the Commission.

Deutsche Telekom AG's main German rivals have filed a complaint in Brussels, urging the Commission to repeal an earlier ruling that allows Telekom to give discounts of up to 49 percent to its corporate clients.

Brussels approved the discounts in June after a lengthy dispute with German Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch and only after winning assurance from Bonn that strict conditions would be met.

The German government had to agree that "at least two licences for the construction or ownership and control of alternative infrastructure" offering telecoms services would have come into force by November.

But the six main companies competing against Telekom in the area of corporate networks now say that the strict conditions set by the European Commission when it approved the rates in June have not been met and should be reviewed.

The complaint was filed by Communications Network International, the Mannesmann unit, Thyssen subsidiary Plus Net, Veba's Meganet, RWE Telliance AG, WorldCom Inc and Viag Interkom, the joint venture of Viag AG and British Telecom.
The complaint threatened to reopen the debate over Telekom's planned discounts, which its rivals say represent a massive abuse of the company's dominant market position.

The dispute also raises uncertainties about the regulatory environment in Germany just weeks before Deutsche Telekom's international share listing and could cast doubt on final approval for Global One, the company's international venture with France Telecom and Sprint Corp.

If Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert sides with the companies that filed the complaint, it could spark a new row between Bonn and Brussels over just how fast Germany is moving to open its telecommunications sector to competition.
This in turn, said industry sources, could cause the Commission to reassess its approval of Global One.
But the German government dismisses as unfounded any charges that it is putting up any obstacles to Deutsche Telekom's competitors.
"We are somewhat behind schedule," said Hoppe. "But there is no doubt that we will exercise a liberal orientation in regulatory matters just as is laid out in the telecommunications law."
